newsitem.title: USA: Local housing groups laud Clinton Section 8 bill.
newsitem.headline: Local housing groups laud Clinton Section 8 bill.

text.p: Representatives of local housing finance agencies on Wednesday said that the Clinton Administration's Section 8 restructuring proposal is definitely a step in the right direction.

"This certainly is a constructive addition to the debate," John Murphy, executive director of the Association of Local Housing Finance Agencies, said in a telephone interview, after U.S. officials proposed a bill to roll back Section 8 housing rents while offering tax incentives to the landlords.

Under the bill, owners of subsidized housing who renegotiate their mortgages would be allowed to stretch out their tax bills that result from the mortgage restructuring over a period of up to 10 years.

"I think the significance of this proposal is that the Department of Housing and Urban Development was able to convince the Treasury Department that there is in fact a tax problem" that any bill must address, Murphy said.
"This helps to move the process forward," he said. "There has not been anything put on the table before this" that addresses the tax problem, Murphy added.
He said a Section 8 bill introduced by Sen. Connie Mack, R-Fla., chairman of the Senate Banking Committee's subpanel on housing opportunity, does not include tax incentives.
Rep. Rick Lazio, R-N.Y., chairman of the House Banking Committee's housing subpanel is expected to introduce a Section 8 bill shortly.
The Clinton bill was announced at a press briefing by HUD Secretary Andrew Cuomo and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.
Another housing industry expert called Clinton's proposed tax incentives "very important."
Without the incentives, owners of Section 8 housing "will do everything they can to avoid tax consequences, so they will delay, postpone and object to restructuring," he said.
The National Association of Counties called the bill "a useful step toward resolving the Section 8 crisis."

"The nation's counties are pleased the administration has taken steps to preserve its investment in affordable multifamily rental housing while at the same time reducing the excessive costs associated with subsidizing these units," Larry Naake, executive director of the group, said.
